# Security awareness training

**GENERATED by tools/generate_awareness_training.py — do not edit.**
Regenerate with `make docs`; `tests/test_awareness_training.py` fails if the
committed file and the generator disagree.

C8, OR-3. ISO/IEC 27001 A 6.3; SOC 2 CC1.4 and CC2.2.

## Why this is derived and not bought

Awareness training is the control easiest to satisfy dishonestly: buy a course,
play a video about phishing, keep the certificates. Every box ticked, and nobody
has learned anything about this system.

So the syllabus is not written. Most of it is **derived from the policy clauses
the software does not enforce** — a distinction `docs/POLICIES.md` already makes,
because a policy claiming an unenforced control is the failure that document
exists to avoid. That distinction is a syllabus with no judgement in it: a clause
the system enforces cannot be got wrong by a person and needs no training, and a
clause only a person upholds is the entire surface this control addresses.

The rest is drawn from **risks with a recorded instance** in
`docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md` — things that went wrong in this codebase rather than
in an industry anecdote. Nobody can dismiss those as not applying to them.

| | |
|---|---|
| Modules derived from unenforced policy clauses | 7 |
| Modules drawn from observed risks | 5 |

## What this document is not

It is not training. There is no learner, no delivery, no completion record with
a name in it, and no evidence that anybody has read a word. OR-3 stays `Process`
for that reason. What is here is the syllabus and the shape of the record; a
person has to deliver it and sign the result.

It also does not set the frequency or the audience. Those are commitments an
organisation makes, so they are left blank below rather than invented.

## Syllabus

### M-AC-P10 — Multi-factor authentication, which this software does not have

**Audience.** Security, and anybody who might assume the software handles it

**Why this is here.** `AC-P10` is a policy clause the software does not enforce — Security does. **The software does not implement MFA.** Where an OIDC provider is configured this is satisfied by delegating to it (AC-P9) and is the recommended arrangement.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Say plainly that local password accounts have no second factor, and that MFA is real only where an OIDC provider is configured and administrative access actually goes through it. Never describe the product as supporting MFA without that qualification — to a customer, in a questionnaire, or in a listing. If you are asked whether it does, the answer is "through your identity provider, and only if your admins sign in that way".

Traces to: `AC-P10` in `docs/POLICIES.md`.

### M-CR-P7 — What the product encrypts, and what your deployment has to

**Audience.** Operations, and anybody who might assume the software handles it

**Why this is here.** `CR-P7` is a policy clause the software does not enforce — Operations does. The product **ships** a TLS terminator with automatic certificate issuance and an 80→443 redirect, and `make check-configs` validates it in CI after the shipped Caddyfile turned out never to have started.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Separate the two. The product ships a TLS terminator with automatic certificates and an 80→443 redirect, validated in CI. The DNS record, the trust chain, and encryption at rest on the disk or volume are the deployment's — DP-3 and DP-4 are `Operator` in the register for exactly that reason. Before answering "is data encrypted at rest", check what the operator did rather than what the chart ships.

Traces to: `CR-P7` in `docs/POLICIES.md`.

### M-SD-P9 — Review before merge is a setting somewhere else

**Audience.** Engineering, and anybody who might assume the software handles it

**Why this is here.** `SD-P9` is a policy clause the software does not enforce — Engineering does. Branch protection and required reviewers are settings on the source host, not properties of this repository, so nothing here can assert it.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Check that branch protection and required reviewers are actually enabled on the source host, and know that nothing in the repository can assert it — the automated gates run regardless of who reviewed. Do not cite "changes are reviewed" as a control without having looked at that console.

Traces to: `SD-P9` in `docs/POLICIES.md`.

### M-IR-P6 — The 72 hours in Article 33, and when the clock starts

**Audience.** Legal, and anybody who might assume the software handles it

**Why this is here.** `IR-P6` is a policy clause the software does not enforce — Legal does. GDPR Article 33's window is a fact; meeting it needs a named person, a decision procedure and a contact, none of which exist here.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Know that the window runs from becoming *aware* of a breach, not from confirming one, and that the assessment is a legal decision needing a named person. Know where the evidence lives: the append-only audit trail, the export, and the subject-access report that can establish who was affected. Escalate on suspicion rather than waiting for certainty, because waiting spends the window.

Traces to: `IR-P6` in `docs/POLICIES.md`.

### M-IR-P7 — The incident plan exists and has never been rehearsed

**Audience.** Security, and anybody who might assume the software handles it

**Why this is here.** `IR-P7` is a policy clause the software does not enforce — Security does. **The plan is written**: `docs/INCIDENT_RESPONSE.md`, by C4; every route, alert, file and capability it names is checked to exist.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Know that `docs/INCIDENT_RESPONSE.md` is thirty steps across detect, triage, contain, eradicate, recover and learn, and that **every lever in it is tested individually and nobody has run them in sequence**. Treat the first real incident as the rehearsal it will be: follow the document, and write down where it was wrong. Know that triage precedes containment because containment destroys evidence.

Traces to: `IR-P7` in `docs/POLICIES.md`.

### M-IR-P8 — After an incident, produce the rule and not only the fix

**Audience.** Security, and anybody who might assume the software handles it

**Why this is here.** `IR-P8` is a policy clause the software does not enforce — Security does. The pre-production review applied precisely this practice to defects, finding by finding: what was found, what it cost, and the rule that keeps it fixed (`REVIEW_FINDINGS.md` indexes it).

**Afterwards, the person can.** Write down what was found, what it cost, and the change that keeps it fixed — the form the pre-production review used for defects (`REVIEW_FINDINGS.md`). A fix without a rule is a fix that gets reverted by the next person who does not know why the code was odd.

Traces to: `IR-P8` in `docs/POLICIES.md`.

### M-IR-P9 — Where to report, and the failure mode of a reporting channel

**Audience.** Security, and anybody who might assume the software handles it

**Why this is here.** `IR-P9` is a policy clause the software does not enforce — Security does. **`SECURITY.md` is written**, by C6: where to report, what to include, what is in scope and what is not, and what a reporter can expect.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Know the address in `SECURITY.md` and what a report should contain, including what you did *not* check. Know that the channel's failure mode is nobody reading it: an address in a file is not a control, and if you own it, say how often you look.

Traces to: `IR-P9` in `docs/POLICIES.md`.

### M-REPORT — How to report something, and why speed beats certainty

**Audience.** Everyone with access to a customer deployment

**Why this is here.** A 6.8. `SECURITY.md` exists and says where to report; the part that has to be true is that somebody is reading the address.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Report a suspected problem through the channel in `SECURITY.md` without first establishing that it is real. State what was checked and what was not — a report saying "this endpoint leaks X, I did not check whether auth catches it" is more useful than silence and cheaper than a confident wrong one.

Traces to: `R-19` in `docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md`, each with a recorded instance.

### M-NEVER-RUN — An artefact nobody has executed is not working, it is untested

**Audience.** Everyone with access to a customer deployment

**Why this is here.** R-8, observed four times: a worker that died on import, a TLS profile rejected by its own validator, a chart that could not install, and a backup script nothing had ever run.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Before claiming something works, say when it last ran and what ran it. Treat "it renders", "it lints" and "it type-checks" as different claims from "it runs".

Traces to: `R-8` in `docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md`, each with a recorded instance.

### M-UNTRUE-DOC — A document that is wrong is worse than a document that is missing

**Audience.** Everyone with access to a customer deployment

**Why this is here.** R-9. For a self-hosted product the documents *are* the product to anybody deciding whether to buy it, and a reader cannot tell which sentence to distrust.

**Afterwards, the person can.** When changing behaviour, find what described the old behaviour and change it in the same commit. Where a claim can be checked mechanically, check it — this repository asserts its documents against the code precisely because good intentions did not hold.

Traces to: `R-9` in `docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md`, each with a recorded instance.

### M-VACUOUS-GUARD — A check that passes for the wrong reason is worse than no check

**Audience.** Everyone with access to a customer deployment

**Why this is here.** R-10. A guard plus false confidence — a suite that reported green while skipping every integration test, a probe that found no violations on a page it never rendered.

**Afterwards, the person can.** For any check you rely on, be able to say what makes it fail. Break it deliberately once and watch it fail; if it does not, the check was not what you thought it was.

Traces to: `R-10` in `docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md`, each with a recorded instance.

### M-CUSTOMER-DATA — What leaves a customer's network, which is nothing

**Audience.** Everyone with access to a customer deployment

**Why this is here.** R-3, and the product's central promise. The vendor receives nothing and there is no setting that changes that; a customer's own configuration is the only thing that sends data anywhere.

**Afterwards, the person can.** Recognise that adding any outbound call — telemetry, a licence check, an error reporter, a CDN font — breaks the claim the product is sold on, and that a test exists to stop it. Know that source code reaches whichever model endpoint the customer configured, and that this makes them a controller with their own obligations.

Traces to: `R-3` in `docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md`, each with a recorded instance.

## What is deliberately not on the syllabus

**Anything the software enforces.** A person cannot choose a signing key at all —
the server generates it — or start a deployment with the portal bypass on
outside development, or accept an unverified webhook. Teaching people to do what
the system already refuses to let them get wrong is how a syllabus teaches its
audience that it is not worth attention. A test fails if a module appears for an
enforced clause.

**Generic material.** Phishing, password reuse and device hygiene are real and
are not specific to this product. If the organisation buys a course for them,
that is sensible and this document does not duplicate it — what it will not do is
present bought material as evidence that anybody understands *this* system.

**Assessment.** Whether a person has learned something is not established by
their having attended. Each module states an outcome somebody can be asked to
demonstrate; turning those into questions is the trainer's job and inventing a
pass mark here would be inventing evidence.
